questions.question: Let G be a group of 35 elements. Then the largest possible size of a subgroup of G other than G itself is _______.
questions.explanation:
By Lagrange's theorem, the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group. Divisors of 35: 1, 5, 7, 35.

Excluding G itself, the largest possible is 7 (a group of order 35 is cyclic and has subgroups of every divisor order).

Answer: 7

S2: Set of all functions from the set[latex]\{0,1,2,...,n^2-1\}[/latex] to the set [latex]\{0, 1, 2 \}[/latex]

options.B: There exists a surjection from S1 to S2

questions.explanation:

- [latex]|S_2|=3^{n^2}[/latex] (each of the [latex]n^2[/latex] inputs has 3 choices).

Equal finite sizes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] a bijection exists (read the matrix entries in order as the function values). A bijection is also a surjection and an injection.

questions.question: Let G=(V,E) be a directed graph where V is the set of vertices and E the set of edges. Then which one of the following graphs has the same strongly connected components as G ?

options.C: [latex]G_{3}=(V,E_{3})[/latex] where [latex]E_{3}\equiv \{(u,v)|[/latex] there is a path of lenth [latex]\leq[/latex] 2 from u to v in E}
options.D: [latex]G_{4}=(V_{4},E)[/latex] where [latex]V_{4}[/latex]  is the set of vertices in G which are not isolated

questions.explanation:
Reversing every edge keeps every cycle (just traversed backwards). If u and v can reach each other in G, they still can in the reversed graph, so the strongly connected components are the same.

The complement graph, the "paths of length [latex]\le[/latex] 2" graph and removing isolated vertices can all change the SCCs.

Answer: [latex]G_2[/latex] with all edges reversed

questions.question:
The probability density function [latex]f(x)[/latex] of a random variable [latex]X[/latex] which takes real values is

[latex] f(x)=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2 \pi}} \exp \left(-\frac{x^{2}}{18}\right), \quad x \in(-\infty,+\infty) [/latex]

Which one of the following statements is correct about the random variable [latex]X[/latex] ?

options.C: [latex]X[/latex] is a Poisson random variable

questions.explanation:
The given density [latex]f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{18}\right)[/latex] has exactly the form of the Gaussian/normal density [latex]f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)[/latex] with mean [latex]\mu=0[/latex] and, matching [latex]2\sigma^2=18\Rightarrow\sigma^2=9\Rightarrow\sigma=3[/latex] (consistent with the [latex]\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}[/latex] normalizing constant).

This is the defining bell-curve density of a normal (Gaussian) random variable with mean [latex]0[/latex] and standard deviation [latex]3[/latex] — it doesn't match the forms of an exponential, Poisson (which is discrete, not even a continuous density), or uniform distribution.

Answer: X is a normal random variable

questions.question:
A quadratic polynomial [latex](x - \alpha)(x - \beta)[/latex] over complex numbers is said to be square invariant if [latex](x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = (x - \alpha^2)(x - \beta^2)[/latex]. Suppose from the set of all square invariant quadratic polynomials we choose one at random.

The probability that the roots of the chosen polynomial are equal is ______. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
[latex](x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=(x-\alpha^2)(x-\beta^2)[/latex] for all [latex]x[/latex] means the root sets [latex]\{\alpha,\beta\}[/latex] and [latex]\{\alpha^2,\beta^2\}[/latex] must be identical (as unordered pairs). Two cases:

Case 1 (each root is individually fixed by squaring): [latex]\alpha^2=\alpha,\ \beta^2=\beta[/latex], forcing each of [latex]\alpha,\beta[/latex] independently into [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] (the only solutions of [latex]z^2=z[/latex]). This gives root-pairs [latex]\{0,0\},\{1,1\},\{0,1\}[/latex] ([latex]3[/latex] distinct polynomials, of which [latex]2[/latex]—[latex]\{0,0\}[/latex] and [latex]\{1,1\}[/latex]—have a repeated root).

Case 2 (roots swap under squaring): [latex]\alpha^2=\beta,\ \beta^2=\alpha[/latex], giving [latex]\alpha^4=\alpha\Rightarrow\alpha(\alpha^3-1)=0[/latex]. Besides the [latex]\alpha=0,1[/latex] solutions already counted, this adds the genuinely new pair of primitive cube roots of unity [latex]\{\omega,\omega^2\}[/latex] (distinct, non-repeated roots).

So there are [latex]4[/latex] distinct square-invariant polynomials total: [latex]\{0,0\},\{1,1\},\{0,1\},\{\omega,\omega^2\}[/latex], of which exactly [latex]2[/latex] ([latex]\{0,0\}[/latex] and [latex]\{1,1\}[/latex]) have equal (repeated) roots.

Probability [latex]=\dfrac24=0.5[/latex]

Answer: 0.5

questions.question: The number of permutations of the characters in LILAC so that no character appears in its original position, if the two L's are indistinguishable, is ______.
questions.explanation:
Positions: 1 L, 2 I, 3 L, 4 A, 5 C. The two L's cannot use positions 1 or 3, so they take 2 of {2, 4, 5}:
- L's at {2, 4}: I, A, C fill 1, 3, 5 with C not at 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3! [latex]-[/latex] 2 = 4
- L's at {2, 5}: fill 1, 3, 4 with A not at 4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4
- L's at {4, 5}: fill 1, 2, 3 with I not at 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4

Total = 12

Answer: 12

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.question:
Suppose an unbiased coin is tossed [latex]6[/latex] times. Each coin toss is independent of all previous coin tosses. Let [latex]E_{1}[/latex] be the event that among the second, fourth, and sixth coin tosses, there are at least two heads. Let [latex]E_{2}[/latex] be the event that among the first, second, third, and fifth coin tosses, there are equal number of heads and tails.
The conditional probability [latex]{P}\left(E_{1} \mid E_{2}\right)[/latex] is equal to ________ (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Toss [latex]4[/latex] and toss [latex]6[/latex] don't appear at all in [latex]E_2[/latex]'s set [latex]\{1,2,3,5\}[/latex], so they remain completely independent, fair (unconditioned) coin flips regardless of [latex]E_2[/latex].

Toss [latex]2[/latex], however, is part of both [latex]E_1[/latex]'s set [latex]\{2,4,6\}[/latex] and [latex]E_2[/latex]'s set [latex]\{1,2,3,5\}[/latex]. Given [latex]E_2[/latex] (exactly [latex]2[/latex] heads among tosses [latex]1,2,3,5[/latex]), by symmetry among these [latex]4[/latex] fair, exchangeable coins, the conditional probability that any particular one of them (in particular, toss [latex]2[/latex]) is heads equals [latex]\dfrac{\binom{3}{1}}{\binom{4}{2}}=\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac12[/latex] — exactly the same as its unconditional probability. So conditioning on [latex]E_2[/latex] doesn't actually bias toss [latex]2[/latex]'s marginal chance of being heads at all.

So, given [latex]E_2[/latex], tosses [latex]2,4,[/latex] and [latex]6[/latex] behave exactly like [latex]3[/latex] independent fair coins. We need [latex]P(\text{at least }2\text{ heads out of }3\text{ fair coin flips})[/latex]:
[latex]P(X\ge2)=\binom{3}{2}(0.5)^3+\binom{3}{3}(0.5)^3=\dfrac{3}{8}+\dfrac{1}{8}=\dfrac{4}{8}=0.5[/latex].

Answer: 0.5

questions.question: Consider a simple undirected unweighted graph with at least three vertices. If [latex]A[/latex] is the adjacency matrix of the graph, then the number of 3-cycles in the graph is given by the trace of

options.C: [latex]A^3[/latex] divided by 3

questions.explanation:
[latex](A^3)_{ii}[/latex] = number of closed walks of length 3 starting at vertex i, i.e. triangles through i, each counted twice (two directions).

In the trace, every triangle appears at each of its 3 vertices [latex]\times[/latex] 2 directions = 6 times.

Number of triangles [latex]=\frac{tr(A^3)}{6}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]A^3[/latex] divided by 6
